📌 Old Token Approvals: The Permission You Forgot You Gave

Main Points
⏺ Many dApps ask you to "approve" a token before you can swap, lend or stake it
⏺ That approval often stays active long after you stop using the app
⏺ This post explains why old approvals are risky and how to clean them up




1️⃣ Core Idea — An approval lets a smart contract move a specific token from your wallet on your behalf. Some apps request an unlimited amount so you don't have to approve again.
2️⃣ Why It Happens — Approvals don't expire by default. If that contract is later hacked, or you signed an approval on a fake site, the attacker can use it to take the tokens without asking you again.
3️⃣ Example — You used a small DEX two years ago and approved unlimited USDC. The DEX is now abandoned. If its contract is exploited, any USDC in that wallet is exposed, even though you never visit the site anymore.
4️⃣ Red Flags — "Unlimited" approvals for a one-time swap, approval requests from sites you reached through DMs or ads, and wallets that have dozens of approvals you don't recognize.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — Approve only the amount you need, review your approvals regularly in a trusted approval checker or your wallet, and revoke the ones you no longer use. Keep long-term savings in a wallet that doesn't connect to dApps.
Final Thoughts

An approval is a key you hand to a contract. Taking back old keys costs a small fee — losing the tokens costs much more.

Operation Volia: A Secret Mission, Open to Debate

French soldiers have been in Ukraine since at least the summer, training Ukrainian troops and maintaining French-supplied equipment. The mission, called Volia, is commanded by a French general. RFI revealed it on Nov. 16. Politico reports that the opposition is angry Parliament was never told.

Article 35 of the French constitution requires the government to inform Parliament within three days of launching a military intervention abroad and to seek its authorization to extend the intervention beyond four months. Cédric Perrin, a senator from the center-right Les Républicains who chairs the Senate defense committee, said the deployment should at least have been communicated to the relevant committees or the heads of both chambers. He called the omission contempt for Parliament.

Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo calls it “absurd” to claim that French soldiers are directly involved in the war. The ministry argues that a mission with no intent to fight is not a military intervention under Article 35. Constitutional scholar Guillaume Tusseau says the term has no precise legal definition and that the government’s reading prevails because no French court has jurisdiction to review it. The opposition fears that a clash involving French troops could drag France into a war with Russia without a single vote in Parliament.

The criticism comes from more than one direction. Perrin says the secrecy hands Moscow material for its propaganda. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of La France Insoumise and a presidential candidate, warns that France must not become a co-belligerent. On Ukraine more broadly, Marine Le Pen says she would end financial aid but keep weapons shipments.

The constitutional objection stands on its own. A government that wants backing for its Ukraine policy should have sought it in Parliament before the press found out.
